description: I am interested in coding, software, data science and passionate about IT and data visualisation.
summary: NASA Earth Jukebox × Chromophonia is an interactive multi-sensory Earth science platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Calibrated directly to official NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS #40509) Earth Now datasets, the application transforms global satellite observations—such as GEOS-FP wind speeds, precipitation, wildfire radiative power, and atmospheric trace gases—into multi-layered soundscapes and music. Built with an accessibility-first architecture for blind and visually impaired users, it features real-time sonification, WCAG AAA high-contrast visuals, keyboard shortcuts, hands-free voice interaction, and webcam hand-tracking powered by MediaPipe AI. Users navigate 12 curated planetary datasets through natural gestures: pointing steers geographical coordinates, pinching probes local sensor measurements, clenched fists silence speech, and hand waves sequentially cycle map layers. An integrated cartoon-inspired voice assistant, Wally, provides real-time scientific explanations, creating an engaging, hands-free bridge between orbital NASA data and human perception.
details:
1. About the Project

Our project is called NASA Earth Jukebox × Chromophonia. The idea is simple: NASA satellite maps can be not only viewed, but also heard. We transform them into music that users can explore through sound, voice, and gestures without looking at the screen.

This is a web application. It uses 18 maps from the NASA SVS “Earth Now Dashboard” gallery (#40509), reads the color of the pixel beneath the cursor, and converts it into a physical measurement: temperature, wind speed, precipitation, air pollution, or sea ice area. This value is then expressed as music. The sound is produced by Kazakh folk instruments (dombra, kobyz, zhetygen, sybyzgy, and shankobyz) and several synthesizers. The application can be controlled with a mouse, keyboard, gestures in front of a webcam, and voice. Voice interaction is supported by an assistant called “Wally,” which understands Russian and English.

2. The Problem

Almost all scientific data about the Earth is visual today. NASA climate maps consist of color scales, legends, and gradients. People who are blind or have low vision cannot explore these maps independently, and there are hundreds of millions of people in this situation worldwide.

However, this data can also be difficult for sighted people to understand. Concentrations of PM2.5, CO, and NOx, as well as wind speed, are difficult to interpret through a complex graph. Hearing, on the other hand, can detect things the eye may miss: rhythm, pitch, timbre, and the direction of sound. We wanted people to be able to literally hear a hurricane or a plume of smoke.

3. The Challenge

We chose the “Earth Jukebox” challenge by the NASA Earth Information Center. The challenge is to create a “jukebox” or sonification system that analyzes EIC visualizations and turns them into soundscapes. The project should combine scientific accuracy, computer vision, sound engineering, and music as an art form.

4. Our Solution

First, the application converts pixels into sound. Using HTML5 Canvas, we read the color and gradient intensity beneath the cursor in real time on any of the 18 maps. Based on NASA’s color scale, we reconstruct the physical value in its original units (°C, m/s, mm/h, µg/m³, ppbv, %) and then convert it into a note and a short eight-step motif.

Instead of a monotonous synthesizer beep, the data is played through five modeled Kazakh instruments and four synthesizers. We call this part “Chromophonia.” Users can choose steppe modes, such as “Qоңыр күй” and “Дала сазы,” or familiar musical scales from around the world.

Each map has its own sound. The wind map produces a whistling sound, the precipitation map sounds like rain, the fire map crackles like burning embers, and the sea ice map rings like crystal. When the cursor reaches the center of a storm or fire, the music becomes louder and faster.

Sound also communicates location on the map. The west is heard in the left earphone, and the east in the right. A click is heard at the coastline, and the phone vibrates (Web Vibration API). The equator is marked by a bell-like chord.

The “Wally” assistant continuously listens for its name, so users do not need to press any buttons. It answers questions about the data in Russian and English and switches between maps and instruments. If the user shows a closed fist to the camera, Wally immediately stops speaking.

5. NASA Research and Data

All data used in the project comes from publicly available NASA sources. The main source is the NASA SVS #40509 gallery, “Earth Now Dashboard.” It contains 18 visualizations divided into several groups.

Four maps are based on the GMAO GEOS-FP weather model: near-surface air temperature (#5147), near-surface wind speed (#5148), precipitation and cloud cover (#5149), and specific humidity (#5150). Another four maps are based on the GMAO GEOS-CF atmospheric composition model: PM2.5 (#5151), surface ozone (#5152), carbon monoxide (#5153), and nitrogen oxides (#5154). The last map clearly shows maritime shipping routes.

The remaining maps are based on NASA Worldview and LANCE satellite observations. These include true-color images from Terra MODIS, nighttime lights from VIIRS Black Marble, the GOES and Himawari geostationary mosaic, active fires detected by VIIRS, GPM IMERG precipitation, sea and land surface temperatures, AMSR2 sea ice, and a five-day full-disk view from NOAA GOES-East and GOES-West (#5120).

In addition to the maps, we use the NASA EONET v3 API. It provides real-time information about natural events, including wildfires, tropical storms, volcanic eruptions, and icebergs.

We also studied the WCAG 2.1 guidelines, approaches to auditory maps for blind users, and the sound of Kazakh instruments, including the rhythms of kui and overtone resonance.

6. Our Workflow

The work was completed in five stages. First, we examined all 18 maps, studying their color palettes, legends, and areas of anomalies. For example, map #5147 shows heat of around +44.8 °C over Arabia; map #5148 shows winds of up to 39.5 m/s in the Southern Ocean and Typhoon Lan; and map #5151 shows smoke from Canadian wildfires reaching 238 µg/m³.

Next, we developed a pixel decoder called decodePixelToDatasetValue. It converts a pixel’s color both into a sensor reading and into musical parameters: MIDI pitch, octave, and filter cutoff frequency.

At the third stage, we built an audio engine using the Web Audio API. All sounds are synthesized directly in the browser, without large audio files. We then integrated voice interaction through the Web Speech API and hand tracking through MediaPipe Hands, adding our own swipe and fist detectors. Finally, we tested accessibility: keyboard controls (arrow keys, spacebar, keys 1–9, M, C, A, F), screen reader support through ARIA live regions, and a high-contrast mode.

7. Technologies

The project is built with JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and CSS3. The interface is developed with React 18 and bundled using Vite 5. The icons are from Lucide React.

The audio system runs on the Web Audio API. We use FM and subtractive synthesis, formant filters for the kobyz and shankobyz, as well as StereoPannerNode, DynamicsCompressorNode, and AnalyserNode for the oscilloscope.

For map analysis, we use OffscreenCanvas. For gesture recognition, we use Google MediaPipe Hands and our own gesture recognizer, which detects pointing, pinching, swiping left and right, a closed fist, and a thumbs-up. Voice interaction is powered by the Web Speech API: SpeechRecognition listens for the word “Wally,” while SpeechSynthesis reads out the responses. Data comes from NASA SVS #40509 and the NASA EONET v3 API.

8. What We Built

The result is a fully functional web application. Its main component is an interactive map. Users can switch between all 18 maps by category, drag markers representing extreme values, and place their own pins to compare different locations. EONET events are marked on the map, while a side panel displays the detected color, its corresponding note, and frequency.

Next to the map is a sonification control panel with three tabs. The first allows users to select an instrument and musical mode, adjust intensity and reverb, and use a kui sequencer and oscilloscope. The second tab displays all 18 measurements for the selected point. The third contains a playlist of seven sound stories in which the application automatically explores the Earth’s major anomalies.

The “Wally” assistant answers questions and navigates to specific locations on command, for example, “Wally, show me the typhoon” or “Wally, switch to Dombra.” Users can move the cursor with their finger, switch maps with a hand swipe, and mute the voice assistant with a closed fist.

9. Innovation and Impact

We have not come across other projects that sonify NASA data using traditional Kazakh music. The sound feels alive: the kobyz conveys the heat of the desert, the sybyzgy evokes ocean winds, and the dombra captures the rhythm of a tropical downpour. The sound depends both on the pixel’s color and on the actual sensor value. The application can be controlled in three ways: with a keyboard and mouse, by voice, or through gestures.

The project is primarily designed for blind and visually impaired users. Students, schoolchildren, and researchers can independently “hear” continents, storms, and air pollution without needing an intermediary. For other users, the music offers an engaging way to learn about the climate while discovering the sound of Kazakh instruments.

10. Team

Zhaniya Nauken — Team Lead. Responsible for the concept, research into NASA data, user experience for blind users, documentation, and the pitch.

Amir Batyrkhanov, Daulet Almagambetov — Sound and Sonification. Developed the audio engine, the timbres of Kazakh instruments, and soundscapes for all 18 maps.

Moldir Zhenispek, Erkebulan Andizhanov — Frontend and Computer Vision. Developed the React interface, map reading through Canvas, draggable markers, and the oscilloscope.

Aisha Moldan — Voice and Gestures. Developed the “Wally” assistant and hand tracking through MediaPipe Hands.

11. Testing and Results

We tested all 18 maps and compared the visible anomalies with the output of the decoder and Wally’s responses. We found no discrepancies in coordinates or color scales. Pixel reading and sound conversion take less than 4 ms, the application maintains 60 frames per second, and the audio has no noticeable delay.

Wally reliably understands commands in Russian and English without requiring users to press buttons. The “fist” gesture interrupts speech in less than 100 ms. A 650 ms pause is set between swipes to prevent accidental map switching.

We also tested the application in a blind-use scenario: using only the keyboard and voice, with the monitor turned off. The user can distinguish land from ocean by sound, locate the equator, and understand the intensity of an anomaly.

12. Future Development

At the moment, we sonify individual frames. In the future, we want to sonify changes over time, such as the movement of a typhoon or smoke plume over ten days. We also plan to integrate high-resolution NASA GIBS imagery so that cities and glaciers become visible when users zoom in. In addition, we want to add MIDI and WAV melody exports and develop a mobile version with spatial audio, vibration, and support for refreshable Braille displays.

13. Sources

1. NASA SVS, gallery #40509 “Earth Now Dashboard”: https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/gallery/earth-now-dashboard/

2. NASA Earth Information Center: https://earth.gov/

3. NASA GMAO, GEOS-FP and GEOS-CF models: https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/

4. NASA Worldview and LANCE: https://worldview.earthdata.nasa.gov/

5. NASA EONET v3 API: https://eonet.gsfc.nasa.gov/api/v3/events

6. NOAA GOES-East and GOES-West, Full Disk (SVS #5120): https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5120

7. W3C Web Audio API: https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/

8. Google MediaPipe Hand Landmarker: https://developers.google.com/mediapipe/solutions/vision/hand_landmarker
